A.explanation: Frequency does not decide if polarisation is possible - both high and low frequency transverse waves can be polarised.

B.explanation: Only transverse waves can be polarised because their oscillations are perpendicular to travel and can be restricted to one plane.

C.explanation: Needing a medium or travelling in a vacuum is true for sound and radio waves but does not explain polarisation.

D.explanation: Wave speed $v$ does not decide if polarisation is possible - fast and slow transverse waves can both be polarised.

hints: Notice the question asks for the reason why one wave can be polarised and the other cannot, not for another difference between radio waves and sound waves.
Recall what polarisation does: it restricts the oscillation direction to a single plane perpendicular to the direction of travel.
Compare the oscillation direction to the travel direction for radio waves and for sound waves to see which type allows more than one plane of oscillation.
walkthrough: Identify the process: polarisation means allowing oscillations in only one plane perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
State the rule: only transverse waves can be polarised, because their oscillations are perpendicular to travel so there are many possible planes around the travel direction.
Explain the contrast: in a longitudinal wave the oscillations are parallel to travel, along the same line as the wave moves, so there is no perpendicular plane to select.
Apply to this item: radio waves are electromagnetic transverse waves with oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to travel, so they can be polarised.
Apply to sound: sound waves in air are longitudinal waves with compressions and rarefactions along the travel direction, so they cannot be polarised.
Therefore the transverse-longitudinal difference is the reason. This is option B.
